demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Thirty-two months ago, on a steep ridge above the Kettle River basin, the weight of a dead pine shifted unexpectedly. Elias had been bracing the timber for the cable winch when the steel tension snapped. The log swung low, catching him in the ribs and pinning his left arm against the rough bark. He felt the sudden, sharp pain flare through his shoulder and side, and the metallic taste of fear as he looked down at the chain-saw operator, Julian, who had stepped too close to catch the line. Julian’s leg was caught in the underbrush, blood darkening the ferns. Elias had been pressed shoulder-to-shoulder with the trunk, trapped in the exact spot where the accident unfolded, watching Julian’s face flatten into shock. In the months that followed, the forest that had been his livelihood turned into a landscape of quiet alarms. When he stood near the edge of the treeline now, his left shoulder would ache with a dull, persistent throb. The evening patrol routes grew too long. The sight of a man in a high-visibility vest, the curve of a forearm against a work glove, would pull Julian’s pale face into his mind. A wave of grief would make his knees buckle. Sometimes, standing in the equipment shed, his own posture would lock—feet planted, shoulders hunched forward, arms braced against an invisible weight. The air would leave him. When the memory returned, a hot, sharp rage would flare in his chest. A deeper grief would feel like drowning. He was certain that there was something fundamentally off about his own hands, something that had drawn the branch down. He could not rely on his own judgment anymore. Every tree looked like a potential threat. Every stranger’s shadow felt like a question he could not answer. Work became a series of narrow corridors and rigid routines. At the ranger station, Elias sat at the far end of the long oak table, his back to the wall. He watched the deputies and contractors move through the door, tracking the angle of their approach, the speed of their steps. When a new seasonal arrived, he kept a respectful distance, refusing to stand within arm’s reach of anyone, even during routine log inspections. He told his wife, Clara, that he was just being cautious, but he knew he was avoiding the shed, the winch house, the steep slopes where a fall could happen again. He stopped driving the timber truck. He stopped checking the load lines. The cabin he and Clara had loved for a decade felt increasingly like a cage. He would lie in bed, jaw clenched, shoulders rigid, unable to let his breathing settle even when the house was quiet and the dogs were asleep. He had come to believe he could no longer do the work that had defined his life for thirty years. He missed the rhythm of his father’s old Spanish forester journals, the way his abuela used to leave a small crucifix on his toolbelt, but the tools now sat dusty in the corner. The decision to seek help came slowly. It was not a single breaking point, but the quiet accumulation of missed inspections, the growing silence between him and his crew, and the way he now flinched when a neighbor’s dog trotted up the driveway. He sat in the waiting room of the community mental health clinic, hands folded tightly in his lap, waiting for his name to be called. What frightened him most was sitting in that office and hearing the truth he already carried: that he was broken. What he hoped for, instead, was a way to walk through the woods again without feeling the phantom weight of the pine, without watching every movement for danger, without the grief that still came, unbidden, whenever the wind moved through the branches.
